Fundamentals, explained

What Is Return on Equity?

How well a company turns shareholders' money into profit — the efficiency scorecard.

So what is it, exactly?

Picture this: two friends each open a sandwich shop with $100,000 of their own savings. A year later, the first shop has earned $20,000 in profit. The second earned $4,000. Same investment, same year — but the first friend's money worked five times harder. That's what return on equity measures.

ROE takes a company's yearly profit and divides it by shareholders' equity — the money investors have put in and left in the business. An ROE of 15% means every $100 of shareholder money produced $15 of profit this year.

Why should you care?

Because when you buy a stock, your money becomes part of that equity — and ROE tells you how hard management makes it work. A consistently high ROE is one of the best signs of a quality business: it means the company doesn't just earn money, it earns money efficiently, year after year.

One friendly warning: a company can inflate its ROE by borrowing heavily — less equity on the books makes the return look bigger. That's why ROE and the debt check travel together. A high ROE with low debt is the real thing. A high ROE with a mountain of debt deserves a raised eyebrow.

Let's make it real

Imagine two companies that each hold $100 million of shareholders' equity. This year, Company A earns $18 million in profit. Company B earns $5 million. Same money invested — very different results.

Company A $18M profit ÷ $100M equity
ROE 18%
Every $100 of shareholder money made $18 this year.
Company B $5M profit ÷ $100M equity
ROE 5%
Every $100 made just $5 — barely beating a savings account.

Company A's management is turning investor money into real returns. Company B's shareholders might fairly ask what their capital is doing all day. ROE won't tell you everything — but it tells you who's working harder with the same dollars.
